newsitem.title: USA: Record numbers of U.S tourists head for Europe, Japan.
newsitem.headline: Record numbers of U.S tourists head for Europe, Japan.

text.p: Renee Stanley is planning a trip to Europe this May that recalls the grand tours enjoyed only by the well-heeled at the turn of the century.

"We're going to take a tour of Europe," said Stanley, a 30-something manager at American Express Travel Related Services in New York. "So, we're going to go to Rome, Florence, Switzerland, Paris and then London."
Along with the cultural attractions of Europe, Stanley may encounter hordes of fellow tourists in this more democratic era of travel.
A booming U.S. economy and strong consumer confidence have helped fuel this explosion of wanderlust among leisure travelers, according to industry officials.
They predict record numbers of Americans will visit Europe and Japan this year. The peak travel season starts next month and will last through September.

Americans are expected to make 9.5 million "citizen visits" to Europe in 1997, up from an estimated 9 million last year, based on data from Jeff Hamblin, chairman of the 26-nation European Travel Commission in the United States.

The number of American visitors to Japan this year is expected to increase about 10 percent to 646,000, the first time the total has exceeded 600,000, according to statistics from the Japan National Tourist Organisation in New York.
Figures for Europe and Japan included people travelling for business and pleasure.
Not surprisingly, consumers feel upbeat about economic conditions. The U.S. economy has entered its seventh year of economic expansion, producing an average of 242,000 jobs per month so far in 1997.
To a lesser extent, attractive air fares and a strong dollar also have contributed to willingness to travel abroad, experts said.
"If those things are going in favour of international travel, then it will be a good year," said Neil Martin, a spokesman for the European Travel Commission.
Indeed, job security ranks high on the list of factors that effect the decision to splurge on overseas travel.

"I don't think that I would make a major trip -- and this trip is pretty costly -- if I didn't feel I've got my job secure because you would take that money and you (would) actually save it in case something happened," Stanley said.
Stanley said she plans to use cash from her tax return to pay for the trip.
Since the beginning of the year, the dollar has appreciated about 12 percent against the German mark and nearly 10 percent against the Japanese yen.
On April 10, the dollar reached its highest level against the yen in more than 4-1/2 years, and hit a level not seen in over three years against the mark.
It has also strengthened against the Italian lira, Swiss and French francs, among other European currencies.

Yet the strength of the dollar is not typically a primary consideration for American tourists unless the currency appreciates dramatically in a short period as it did when the Mexican peso was devalued in December 1994, according to industry sources.
"The currency situation is not one of the top reasons people decide which country to go to," Martin said. "It may be one of the factors, but it will not be the most important factor."

The number of Americans visiting Japan, especially leisure travelers, decreased in 1993 and 1994 when the yen was expensive, based on data from the Japan National Tourist Organisation. But the number of Americans travelling to Japan began to recover in September 1995 as the dollar rebounded.

The dollar sank to a post World War II low on April 19, 1995. At that time, Americans travelling in Japan had to pay the equivalent of $4.65 for a McDonald's Big Mac hamburger compared with $2.32 (average price including tax) at home, according to The Economist magazine's annual "Big Mac Index" that tracks the price of the deluxe burger in countries around the world.
By April 1997 however, the index showed that a Big Mac cost the equivalent of $2.34 in Japan compared with $2.42 (average price including tax) in the United States.

"After long years of the high yen...it's now very deeply imprinted that Japan is very expensive," said Hiroko Tani, deputy director of the New York office of the Japan National Tourist Organisation. "I want more Americans really to find out how Japan is a bargain right now."
